title: AI Supply Chain — Company Dossiers
summary: Company chapters pinned to the AI chain — 69 companies across 7 layers including the Tier-1/2 hardware tier. Includes the interdependency analysis, a chokepoint map, a second-opinion section (pricing power, domicile hedging, demand side, EUR/USD), the Power & Pixels barbell and the Germany-ready €10k Sparplan (stress-aware revision with cash buffer). Figures verified against Q2 FY2027 Nvidia, the Oct 28-29, 2026 big-tech prints and Vertiv's Q3 2026.
disclaimer: Informational and educational content, not investment advice. All figures are as of late October 2026 and age quickly — check the primary source before acting. Addons cannot open external links, so source URLs are shown as selectable text.

layers.name: Raw materials & equipment
layers.description: The machines that make machines: high-purity silicon wafers, semiconductor gases, rare earths — and EUV lithography, where ASML holds a de facto monopoly. The slowest-moving layer, and the most geopolitically concentrated.

layers.name: Silicon & fabrication
layers.description: Design and fabrication: fabless architects (Nvidia, AMD), the IP and EDA layer that designs every chip (Arm, Synopsys, Cadence), the foundry that prints them (TSMC), advanced packaging (TSMC CoWoS, ASE, Amkor) and the memory makers whose HBM sits beside every accelerator die (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung) — plus the NAND flash tier that stores what inference reads (SanDisk, Kioxia). The physical bottleneck of the AI boom.

layers.name: Components & server assembly (Tier-1/2)
layers.description: The unpacked physical layer: two very different businesses. Toll collectors at scarce nodes — IC substrates (Ibiden, Unimicron, Tripod), high-density power supplies (Delta, Lite-On), high-end cooling — earn real pricing power from 2-3 year lead times. Thin-margin assemblers — Taiwanese ODMs (Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron), Super Micro, Celestica — have giant backlogs but single-digit margins. Interconnect and optics (Amphenol, Marvell, Arista, Coherent, Lumentum, Fabrinet) sit between the two.

layers.name: Compute infrastructure
layers.description: Hyperscalers and neoclouds that own the data centers and rent out compute. They convert capex guidance into orders for everything upstream.

layers.name: Power & physical plant (cross-cutting)
layers.description: Electricity and physical hardware behind the compute: PPAs with nuclear, gas and renewable generators; grid equipment and cooling. Demand is driven by layer 3, but the bills are paid before any model monetizes — which is exactly the appeal.

layers.name: Data & curation
layers.description: Sourcing, licensing, cleaning and labeling training data, plus RLHF labor. Mostly private (Scale AI, in-house teams); the listed names are thin and should be read as sentiment proxies.

layers.name: Models & applications
layers.description: Foundation labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta) and the applications built on their APIs. Where the capex is supposed to turn into revenue.

companies.name: ASML Holding
companies.role: Sole supplier of EUV lithography — every leading-edge AI chip is printed on ASML machines. High-NA EUV is the gate for node transitions beyond the current generation; there is no second source.

kpis.label: Net bookings
kpis.watch: Two consecutive quarters of collapsing orders telegraph foundry capex cuts 12-18 months before wafer output falls.

kpis.label: China revenue share
kpis.watch: Export-control changes swing both demand timing and sentiment.

kpis.label: High-NA adoption
kpis.watch: Ramp pace sets the length of the next equipment cycle.

companies.readThrough: ASML orders are the chain's earliest upstream signal: they land roughly a year before wafer output and two before accelerator shipments. If ASML bookings roll over while hyperscaler capex still looks strong, believe ASML.
risks: Export controls (US/NL) directly limit addressable demand
Lumpy order timing makes quarters noisy

companies.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
companies.role: Fabricates roughly 90% of the world's most advanced processors and controls CoWoS advanced packaging — the step that binds HBM to accelerator dies and has repeatedly been the industry's binding constraint on AI chip shipments.

kpis.label: AI accelerator revenue guidance
kpis.watch: TSMC guides its own AI revenue CAGR; any cut is the strongest negative signal available for the whole chain.

kpis.label: CoWoS capacity expansion
kpis.watch: Packaging gates how many accelerators ship regardless of wafer supply. Capacity adds are demand-confirmation.

kpis.label: Next-node ramp (N2/A16)
kpis.watch: Node transitions drive both pricing power and the next capex wave upstream.

companies.readThrough: TSMC's monthly revenue and guidance are the cleanest read on real AI hardware demand — it books revenue when chips are made, before hyperscalers report anything.

companies.name: NVIDIA
companies.role: Designs the dominant AI accelerators (Blackwell Ultra shipping, Rubin next) and owns the CUDA software moat. In Q2 FY2027, data center was 92% of revenue — this company is the AI buildout, priced.
upstream: cooling and power gear inside its own racks
customers: Hyperscalers — $48.7B of $89B data center revenue, +102% YoY

kpis.label: Data Center revenue
kpis.value: $89.0B in Q2 FY2027 (+117% YoY); $96.2B total revenue
kpis.watch: Deceleration vs. hyperscaler capex guidance. ACIE is now the marginal demand — watch its growth rate first.

kpis.label: Hyperscale vs. ACIE mix
kpis.watch: If debt-funded neoclouds (part of ACIE) crack first, demand mix shifts back to slower hyperscaler growth.

kpis.label: Forward guidance
kpis.watch: Guidance below capex-implied demand is what triggered the October 2026 hardware-layer repricing.

companies.readThrough: Nvidia's quarterly print is the chain's cash-register tape: it confirms or denies that hyperscaler capex guidance actually converts into orders. Everything downstream of it — TSMC packaging, HBM pricing, cooling demand — is repriced around this print.
risks: A handful of hyperscalers plus neoclouds make up most demand
Custom silicon (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Meta MTIA) takes share
China data center compute is now excluded from guidance (<1% of DC revenue)

companies.name: Broadcom
companies.role: Supplies the networking silicon and optics behind AI clusters (Tomahawk/Jericho switches) and designs custom accelerators (XPUs) for hyperscalers — the second source that grows whenever a customer tries to reduce Nvidia dependence.

kpis.label: AI revenue growth
kpis.value: Watch the quarterly AI revenue line
kpis.watch: Compare against Nvidia's growth: faster = custom silicon is taking share.

kpis.label: Custom accelerator backlog
kpis.watch: New XPU wins lock 2-3 years of revenue — announcements matter more than quarters.

kpis.label: Ethernet vs InfiniBand
kpis.value: Ethernet gaining share in AI clusters
kpis.watch: Continued Ethernet adoption widens Broadcom's addressable market.

companies.readThrough: Broadcom is the cleanest public read on the de-Nvidia-fication trade: it wins when hyperscalers hedge their accelerator supply, so its growth rate is a share-shift indicator, not just a demand indicator.
risks: Concentration in a few custom-ASIC programs

companies.name: Micron Technology
companies.role: One of three HBM suppliers (with SK Hynix and Samsung). HBM is stacked DRAM bonded beside each accelerator die — the most supply-constrained component of the AI bill of materials, priced through long-term contracts.

kpis.label: HBM sold out?
kpis.watch: HBM sold out into the next year = pricing power intact. First inventory build = cycle turn.

kpis.label: HBM share vs SK Hynix
kpis.watch: Nvidia qualification for each HBM generation decides share shifts between Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung.

kpis.label: Capex vs. bit growth
kpis.watch: Disciplined capex keeps memory pricing high; capacity overbuild ends the boom.

companies.readThrough: Memory is the chain's boom-bust amplifier: HBM margins are spectacular at the top and the first thing to collapse if AI capex pauses. Micron's bookings are a five-quarter leading indicator for the memory cycle.
risks: Memory is inherently cyclical — record margins invite supply

companies.name: SK Hynix
companies.role: The HBM market leader and Nvidia's primary HBM partner — arguably the single most supply-constrained company in the AI chain. Listed in Seoul; no liquid US ADR, so many EU retail investors can only participate indirectly.

kpis.label: HBM revenue share
kpis.watch: HBM as % of total revenue: the higher, the more AI leverage and the more cycle risk.

kpis.label: HBM4 qualification
kpis.watch: Whoever qualifies first for Nvidia's HBM4 sets pricing for the generation.

companies.readThrough: When SK Hynix says HBM is sold out, the bottleneck for the whole chain has moved elsewhere (usually TSMC packaging). Watch the two in sequence.

companies.name: Microsoft
companies.role: Hyperscaler (Azure, $33.2B/quarter, +48% YoY) and the main compute landlord for OpenAI — it holds an estimated 27% equity stake in the OpenAI Group, making it the closest listed proxy for the largest private lab.
upstream: power contracts (incl. Constellation's Three Mile Island restart)

kpis.label: Azure growth
kpis.value: +48% YoY in Q1 FY2027; guided to 49-50%
kpis.watch: Deceleration while capex keeps rising is the bear case; acceleration vindicates the buildout.

kpis.label: Capex and free cash flow
kpis.value: $45.2B quarterly capex; ~$170B FY2027 guide; FCF still positive at $18.6B
kpis.watch: Microsoft is the only one of the big three that stayed FCF-positive in October 2026 — if that flips, the whole sector narrative changes.

kpis.label: OpenAI stake marks
kpis.watch: OpenAI's confidential S-1 draft re-prices Microsoft's stub on every valuation headline.

companies.readThrough: Microsoft is the chain's proof point that AI capex can coexist with positive free cash flow — and its OpenAI stake is the main public vehicle for exposure to the largest private lab. Both roles are on the same scorecard.
risks: Capacity shortages (delayed third-party data-center deliveries trimmed Q1 capex)

companies.name: Amazon
companies.role: AWS ($46.0B/quarter, +39% YoY, 38.7% operating margin) is the largest cloud by revenue; Amazon is also Anthropic's anchor backer and builds Trainium custom silicon to dilute Nvidia dependence.

kpis.label: Free cash flow
kpis.watch: Q3 capex $77.3B; 2026 capex ~$220B and 2027 guided significantly higher — FCF stays negative until capex growth stops.

kpis.label: AWS growth and margin
kpis.watch: AWS margin is what ultimately funds the capex; margin compression plus capex growth is the double-warning.

kpis.label: Anthropic stake
kpis.watch: Anthropic's future IPO/valuation marks revalue the stake and the AWS backlog.

companies.readThrough: Amazon is the clearest live experiment in the capex-vs-FCF trade-off: the market rewarded 39% AWS growth but punished the negative FCF with a ~7.5% drop. Watch how far investors tolerate this trade.

companies.name: Alphabet
companies.role: The only fully vertically integrated player: hyperscaler (Cloud +103% to $30.7B), frontier lab (Gemini, 1B app users) and chip designer (TPU) in one. Gemini trains on its own silicon.

kpis.label: Free cash flow
kpis.watch: Capex $51.4B/quarter, 2027 guided significantly higher; buybacks halted and equity issued. FCF is the thesis test.

kpis.label: Search vs AI Mode monetization
kpis.value: AI Mode queries monetize worse than classic search
kpis.watch: The cannibalization question: watch paid-click economics in Search each quarter — this is the industry's core monetization risk in miniature.

kpis.label: Cloud backlog
kpis.watch: Backlog conversion pace; $8.66B equity losses (incl. Anthropic) also hit net income.

companies.readThrough: Alphabet's Oct 28 print was the trigger of the October 2026 repricing: revenue grew 25% (fine), but negative FCF plus AI cannibalizing search broke the 'AI is free growth' story. Its record 13.7% drop is the event the whole chain now trades against.
risks: TPU external sales strategy is unresolved

companies.name: Meta Platforms
companies.role: Open-weights model leader (Llama) and one of the largest capex spenders. Unusual position: it buys compute at hyperscaler scale but has no external cloud to sell the surplus — monetization must come through its own ad products.

kpis.label: Capex vs. ad revenue
kpis.value: Oct 2026 quarter: first net cash outflow since 2012 (reported)
kpis.watch: The ratio of capex growth to ad-revenue growth — when capex outgrows ads, the stock reprices.

kpis.label: Llama adoption
kpis.watch: Open-weights strategy pays off only if the ecosystem builds on Llama rather than OpenAI/Anthropic APIs.

companies.readThrough: Meta is the purest test of whether AI monetization can keep up with capex inside a single company: no cloud revenue to offset the spend, just ads.
risks: Negative FCF with no cloud business to absorb the spend
Open-weights thesis diluted by rivals' stronger models

companies.name: CoreWeave
companies.role: Pure-play AI cloud: rents GPU capacity to AI labs and enterprises, financed largely with debt secured against GPUs. The archetypal neocloud and a large part of Nvidia's ACIE demand segment.

kpis.label: Cost of debt
kpis.watch: Refinancing cost is the whole business model; rising yields with GPU collateral values falling is the failure mode.

kpis.label: Backlog concentration
kpis.watch: A few mega-contracts can carry the backlog — one non-renewal changes the story.

kpis.label: GPU utilization and depreciation
kpis.watch: Contract terms vs. useful life of the GPUs; depreciation outrunning contract revenue is the trap.

companies.readThrough: Neoclouds are the chain's leverage layer: their backlog strength confirms ACIE demand is real, while their bond yields measure how nervous credit markets are about AI. The group fell sharply (~−30% reported) in the October 2026 sell-off — the first domino if AI demand pauses.

companies.name: OpenAI (private)
companies.role: Creator of ChatGPT and the demand anchor behind much of the chain's compute buildout. Private (public benefit corporation after restructuring); Microsoft holds ~27%. A confidential draft S-1 has been filed, with market consensus pointing to a listing around 2027.

kpis.label: Revenue run-rate
kpis.watch: Run-rate vs. compute commitments is the single most important number in the AI economy right now.

kpis.label: Compute commitments
kpis.watch: Commitments being renegotiated down would be the first genuine AI-demand crack.

kpis.label: IPO timing
kpis.watch: A listing converts proxy exposure (MSFT) into direct exposure and re-prices both.

companies.readThrough: Every capex dollar in this chain is ultimately a bet that OpenAI-class demand is durable. Its revenue disclosures and IPO progress are the chain's upside scenario.

sources.title: OpenAI corporate updates / SEC filings via press

companies.name: Anthropic (private)
companies.role: Creator of Claude; enterprise-focused frontier lab backed by Amazon and Google, which also serve as its primary compute providers — a loop where venture funding recycles into AWS/GCP revenue. A confidential draft S-1 has been filed.

kpis.label: Revenue/valuation marks
kpis.watch: Google's Q3 equity losses (incl. Anthropic) show how swings already hit public balance sheets.

kpis.label: IPO progress
kpis.watch: A listing would give both AMZN and GOOGL shareholders a direct benchmark for their stakes.

companies.readThrough: Anthropic is the strongest evidence for the equity-plus-cloud model: the lab's spend flows back to its backers, so its success compounds both stakes at once.

companies.name: Appen
companies.role: One of the few listed data-labeling firms — the public representative of a layer whose real players (Scale AI, in-house teams, click-work platforms) are private. A sentiment proxy, not a structural holding.

kpis.label: Revenue trend
kpis.watch: Shrinking model-training budgets show up here first; growth means the data layer still commands premium spend.

kpis.label: Contract wins
kpis.watch: Generative AI is automating parts of annotation — watch whether Appen captures the RLHF wave or loses to it.

companies.readThrough: The data layer is the least investable link in the chain. Read Appen as a leading indicator of data-spend direction, not as portfolio material.

companies.name: Vertiv
companies.role: The liquid-cooling and power-management specialist of the data center. Next-generation chips run too hot for air cooling, forcing retrofits — Vertiv's core demand driver, and one of the tightest physical bottlenecks in the buildout.

kpis.label: Backlog and book-to-bill
kpis.value: Q3 2026: organic orders +100%+, FY guidance raised to $14.65B revenue
kpis.watch: Order growth above 100% confirms the retrofit wave is still accelerating; watch the first quarter it decelerates.

kpis.label: Revenue and EPS growth
kpis.watch: Growth rates are the proof the bottleneck pricing is real; the stock jumped 16.5% on the print.

kpis.label: Liquid cooling revenue mix
kpis.watch: Rising mix = priced-up product cycle; slowing means air-cooling legacy drag.

companies.readThrough: Vertiv sells into every rack regardless of whose chip sits inside — it is the chip-agnostic way to own the buildout. Its orders lead hyperscaler equipment spending by a quarter or two.
risks: Cyclical exposure to data-center construction pauses
Competition from Schneider and in-house designs

companies.name: Eaton
companies.role: Switchgear, transformers and power distribution — the equipment between the grid and the GPU. Transformer lead times stretched to multi-year during the buildout, making Eaton's backlog a proxy for how fast data centers can actually connect to power.

kpis.label: Electrical Americas backlog
kpis.watch: Multi-year backlog = visibility; backlog growth decelerating while data-center announcements keep coming means grid-pacing constraints.

kpis.label: Transformer lead times
kpis.watch: Lead times contracting from record highs signals the equipment bottleneck is easing — good for data centers, less pricing power for Eaton.

companies.readThrough: Eaton's backlog is the best available public gauge of the physical connection bottleneck: power can be contracted and chips delivered, but without switchgear nothing runs.

companies.name: Constellation Energy
companies.role: The largest US nuclear operator, and the template for the AI power deal: a 20-year PPA to restart Three Mile Island for Microsoft. Hyperscalers pay premium, fixed-rate prices for carbon-free 24/7 power — the most contractually insulated cash flows in the chain.

kpis.label: PPA announcements
kpis.watch: Each new hyperscaler PPA secures years of fixed revenue and validates the premium nuclear model.

kpis.label: Nuclear fleet output
kpis.watch: Uptime on the existing fleet is the free option; restarts add capacity at known cost.

companies.readThrough: Constellation converts the AI power scramble into contracted, inflation-protected revenue. It is the first name paid in the chain — which is exactly why it trades at an AI premium too.
risks: Valuation already assumes the PPA wave continues

companies.name: Vistra
companies.role: Independent power producer with a gas and nuclear fleet in ERCOT and other competitive markets — direct exposure to power prices, which data-center demand keeps pushing up.

kpis.label: Realized power prices
kpis.watch: Merchant exposure means power prices flow straight to earnings — the purest data-center-demand play in utilities.

kpis.label: Fleet expansion/deals
kpis.watch: Acquiring generation capacity near data-center corridors extends the growth runway.

companies.readThrough: Vistra is the high-beta expression of AI power demand: more upside than regulated utilities if demand keeps rising, more downside if the buildout pauses.

companies.name: NextEra Energy
companies.role: The largest US utility by market cap and its biggest renewables developer. Regulated rate-base growth (legally allowed returns) plus a renewables pipeline that data centers need to hit green-energy targets.

kpis.label: Renewables backlog
kpis.watch: Contracted renewables backlog is the growth engine; data-center PPAs extend it.

kpis.label: Rate-base growth
kpis.watch: Approved rate increases fund the grid investment — the regulated half of the hedge.

companies.readThrough: NextEra is the defensive anchor of the power sleeve: slower than CEG/VST but with regulated returns that don't depend on AI demand holding up.

companies.name: EQT Corporation
companies.role: The largest US natural gas producer. Every gigawatt of on-site gas generation for data centers increases structural demand for EQT's molecules — the bridge-fuel thesis in equity form.

kpis.label: Realized gas prices
kpis.watch: Commodity exposure is the point: data-center demand tightens the market, prices follow.

kpis.label: Data-center supply deals
kpis.watch: Direct gas-to-data-center contracts would upgrade the story from commodity to contracted growth.

companies.readThrough: EQT is the cheapest way to own the AI power demand story — a commodity producer with structural demand growth, trading at value multiples with a dividend.

companies.name: Williams Companies
companies.role: Natural gas pipelines and storage. Data centers must be built near fiber and power; on-site gas generation requires pipeline connectivity — Williams owns the pipes that connect the molecules to the megawatts.

kpis.label: Contracted capacity growth
kpis.watch: Fee-based, take-or-pay contracts make revenue stable; new data-center pipeline laterals add growth without commodity risk.

kpis.label: Dividend coverage
kpis.watch: High-yield midstream: coverage ratio determines whether the income is safe during downturns.

companies.readThrough: Williams is the toll road between the gas field and the data center — fee-based cash flows with less commodity swing than EQT, higher yield than utilities.
risks: Volume risk if gas demand stalls

companies.name: Ibiden
companies.role: Maker of the advanced IC package substrates (ABF) that sit between the chip die and the board. AI accelerators need the industry's largest, highest-layer-count substrates — a quiet bottleneck that gates every GPU ramp.

kpis.label: Substrate capacity expansion
kpis.watch: New substrate capacity lands 2-3 years after announcement; lead times are the tell.

kpis.label: AI substrate mix
kpis.watch: Rising AI share = pricing power; falling means the substrate crunch eased.

companies.readThrough: Substrate supply is one of the physical gates on accelerator output — when substrate lead times stretch, Nvidia shipment guidance is capped regardless of wafer supply.

companies.name: Unimicron
companies.role: Taiwan's largest PCB/substrate maker; supplies the ultra-high-density boards and substrates inside AI servers and switches, alongside Ibiden and Tripod.

kpis.label: AI product revenue share
kpis.watch: AI boards carry premium margins; mix shift is the whole equity story.

kpis.label: Utilisation rates
kpis.watch: High utilisation with tight supply means price increases stick.

companies.readThrough: PCB and substrate makers sit at the roof of every AI server — their order books lead ODM assembly by a quarter.

companies.name: Tripod Technology
companies.role: PCB supplier focused on AI server and networking boards — switch line cards and server motherboards that must route enormous data rates without signal loss.

kpis.label: AI server board revenue
kpis.watch: Tracks the ODM build rate a quarter ahead.

kpis.label: Gross margin
kpis.watch: High-layer-count boards command premium pricing; margin is the pricing-power proxy.

companies.readThrough: A second-order Taiwan read: Tripod's orders confirm ODM build plans before the assemblers report.

companies.name: Amphenol
companies.role: Supplies the high-speed copper cabling assemblies and connectors — and increasingly optical transceivers — that link thousands of GPUs into one fabric. Interconnect content per rack grows with every GPU generation.

kpis.label: IT datacom growth
kpis.watch: The cleanest public measure of AI interconnect demand.

kpis.label: AI-related orders
kpis.watch: Content-per-rack growth compounds even if GPU unit growth slows.

companies.readThrough: Amphenol is the 'wiring' play: agnostic to which accelerator wins, paid per rack built. Its datacom growth reads through to real build rates.

companies.name: Marvell Technology
companies.role: Optical DSPs for 800G/1.6T links, plus custom accelerator silicon — the optical-engine counterpart to Broadcom's switching franchise.

kpis.label: Data centre revenue mix
kpis.watch: Optical DSP demand tracks cluster scale-out; a stall precedes ODM slowdowns.

kpis.label: Custom silicon bookings
kpis.watch: Each win locks multi-year revenue and confirms the de-Nvidia-fication trend.

companies.readThrough: Marvell reads the optical layer of the fabric: when clusters stop growing, DSP orders fall first.

companies.name: Super Micro Computer
companies.role: US-based rack-scale integrator: builds the actual AI server boxes and direct-to-liquid-cooled racks that Nvidia sells as DGX/HGX-class systems. The listed US alternative to the Taiwanese ODMs.

kpis.label: Gross margin vs. volume
kpis.watch: ODM economics: volume growth with collapsing margin is the classic trap.

kpis.label: Backlog and customer concentration
kpis.watch: A few mega-customers can carry the backlog; one leaving changes the story.

companies.readThrough: Super Micro converts GPU allocations into completed racks — its shipments are the physical 'delivery' signal of the AI buildout.

companies.name: Foxconn / Hon Hai
companies.role: The world's largest electronics assembler and the biggest builder of Nvidia's GB200/GB300-class AI racks; expanding assembly into Mexico and the US to shorten the Taiwan exposure.

kpis.label: AI server revenue
kpis.watch: The single best public gauge of rack assembly volume.

kpis.label: Non-Taiwan capacity
kpis.watch: Mexico/US lines are the geographic hedge in progress.

companies.readThrough: Foxconn is the assembly chokepoint in company form: over 90% of advanced AI racks pass through Taiwanese ODMs, and Foxconn is the largest of them.
risks: Concentration in a handful of platform programmes

companies.name: Quanta Computer
companies.role: Top-tier AI server ODM assembling hyperscaler and Nvidia platform racks; one of the small group of Taiwanese assemblers that can build at AI scale.

kpis.label: AI server revenue share
kpis.watch: Mix shift from laptops to AI servers is the margin story.

kpis.label: Capacity expansion
kpis.watch: Global capacity buildout is both growth and geopolitical hedging.

companies.readThrough: Quanta's AI server guidance is a direct read on hyperscaler rack orders, a quarter ahead of the capex headlines.

companies.name: Wistron
companies.role: AI server ODM and liquid-cooling module supplier; assembles racks for hyperscalers and supplies thermal assemblies into the same buildout.

kpis.label: AI server growth
kpis.watch: The third-largest ODM read after Foxconn and Quanta.

kpis.label: Cooling module revenue
kpis.watch: Liquid-cooling modules are the higher-margin adjacency.

companies.readThrough: Wistron couples assembly and thermal content — it earns twice from the liquid-cooling transition.

companies.name: Modine Manufacturing
companies.role: Industrial-scale chillers and air handlers for data centres — the second listed pure-play cooling name behind Vertiv, critical for racks above 100kW where air cooling fails.

kpis.label: Data-centre backlog
kpis.watch: Backlog growth confirms the cooling retrofit wave beyond Vertiv.

kpis.label: Thermal segment margin
kpis.watch: Data-centre mix carries higher margins than legacy HVAC.

companies.readThrough: Modine is the diversification away from Vertiv concentration in the cooling sleeve — same demand driver, smaller backlog.

companies.name: AAON
companies.role: Air-handling units and chillers moving into data-centre thermal management; a smaller, US-domiciled cooling beneficiary of the same air-to-liquid transition.

kpis.label: Data-centre orders
kpis.watch: The new demand line; growth confirms the segment is real.

kpis.label: Margins
kpis.watch: Capacity ramp costs vs. pricing power.

companies.readThrough: AAON is a smaller-cap expression of the cooling thesis with more execution risk than Modine or Vertiv.

companies.name: Delta Electronics
companies.role: Dominant supplier of the high-density power supply units inside AI server racks — the bricks that convert grid AC into the clean DC feeding Nvidia and AMD chips. Also supplies power and thermal infrastructure for data centres.

kpis.label: AI power revenue share
kpis.watch: PSU content per rack rises with each GPU generation as wattage climbs.

kpis.label: Data-centre power segment
kpis.watch: Grid-to-chip power products are the higher-margin adjacency.

companies.readThrough: Delta and Lite-On together control most of the AI server PSU market — a supply hiccup here halts rack assembly even when GPUs arrive.

companies.name: Lite-On Technology
companies.role: Second pillar of the AI server PSU market alongside Delta — power supply bricks and power shelves for GPU racks.

kpis.label: AI power revenue
kpis.watch: Same demand driver as Delta; relative share shifts matter.

kpis.label: Margin trend
kpis.watch: Power shelves at AI density command premium pricing.

companies.readThrough: A high-wattage rack needs two PSU suppliers by design — Lite-On is the second-source read on rack power demand.

companies.name: Schneider Electric
companies.role: French energy-management giant: low- and medium-voltage distribution, UPS, cooling and racks for data centres. The EU-listed alternative to Eaton with order backlogs reportedly stretching past 2028.

kpis.label: Data-centre backlog
kpis.watch: Backlogs past 2028 insulate revenue from short-term tech budget cuts.

kpis.label: Organic growth in energy management
kpis.watch: Electrification demand is the structural driver beyond data centres.

companies.readThrough: Schneider is the European, euro-denominated way to own the grid-to-chip power node without USD exposure — and one of the 'Western-domiciled 60%' in the dialogue's geographic hedge.

companies.name: Siemens
companies.role: Grid technology, switchgear and industrial automation; the electrification backbone behind data-centre grid connections in Europe.

kpis.label: Smart Infrastructure orders
kpis.watch: Electrification orders are the grid-buildout proxy.

kpis.label: Data-centre exposure commentary
kpis.watch: Growing explicit AI demand disclosure would re-rate the segment.

companies.readThrough: Siemens is broader and slower than Eaton — the diversified European grid play rather than a pure AI beneficiary.

companies.name: Shin-Etsu Chemical
companies.role: The world's largest supplier of 300mm silicon wafers and photoresists — every advanced chip starts on Shin-Etsu material.

kpis.label: Wafer shipment volumes
kpis.watch: Wafers lead chip output by a quarter; the quietest leading indicator in the chain.

kpis.label: Photoresist pricing
kpis.watch: EUV-era resist demand grows per wafer.

companies.readThrough: Shin-Etsu volume is wafers consumed — an output-side read on fab utilisation, unaffected by which chip designer wins.

companies.name: Linde
companies.role: Supplies the semiconductor-grade gases — nitrogen, argon, neon mixtures — without which fabs cannot etch or cool. Long-term on-site contracts make revenue visible.

kpis.label: Electronics segment growth
kpis.watch: Tracks fab utilisation directly.

kpis.label: On-site contract wins
kpis.watch: Multi-decade take-or-pay contracts at new fab sites are the growth engine.

companies.readThrough: Linde's electronics volumes are a clean read on fab activity; new on-site contracts mark where fabs are being built next.

companies.name: Advanced Micro Devices
companies.role: The clear number two in AI accelerators (Instinct MI-series). Its share gains are the main competitive check on Nvidia pricing — and a genuine alternative source for hyperscalers hedging supply.

kpis.label: Data-centre GPU revenue
kpis.watch: The single best measure of whether Nvidia's pricing power is eroding.

kpis.label: ROCm software adoption
kpis.watch: Hardware is competitive; the software gap is the constraint.

companies.readThrough: AMD's success is the chain's only real de-concentration force at the accelerator layer — watch it as a Nvidia-share story, not just a demand story.

companies.name: Arm Holdings
companies.role: The instruction-set architecture inside nearly every mobile chip and a growing share of custom data-centre silicon (Grace, Graviton, Axion, MTIA-class designs). Royalties on every chip — the purest IP toll in the industry.

kpis.label: Royalty revenue growth
kpis.watch: Tracks total chip volumes across every end market.

kpis.label: Data-centre design wins
kpis.watch: Custom Arm-based accelerators are the share-transfer signal.

companies.readThrough: Arm earns whether Nvidia or the hyperscalers' custom silicon wins — the cleanest expression of the de-Nvidia-fication trend.

companies.name: Synopsys
companies.role: Leader of the EDA duopoly: chip-design software with 90%+ combined share alongside Cadence, plus semiconductor IP. No advanced chip — Nvidia, AMD, TPU, custom ASIC — gets designed without it. Arguably the deepest moat in the entire chain.

kpis.label: Backlog / bookings
kpis.watch: Design starts lead the whole chain by 18-24 months.

kpis.label: China export restrictions
kpis.watch: Controls on EDA tools are a direct revenue lever.

companies.readThrough: EDA bookings are the earliest leading indicator in the world of AI silicon — design starts happen two years before chips ship.

companies.name: Cadence Design Systems
companies.role: The other half of the EDA duopoly, strong in custom/analog and increasingly in system-level AI design (hardware verification, packaging design for advanced nodes).

kpis.label: Backlog growth
kpis.watch: Same leading signal as Synopsys: design activity two years ahead of shipments.

kpis.label: AI-driven product mix
kpis.watch: Verification and packaging software intensity grows with AI chip complexity.

companies.readThrough: Second EDA leader — both names together are the 'sell tools to everyone' position, indifferent to which chip wins.

companies.name: Samsung Electronics
companies.role: The third HBM supplier, a leading-edge foundry (2nm ambitions) and the only company that spans memory, logic and packaging. Currently lagging SK Hynix in HBM qualification — which is exactly why it is the swing factor.

kpis.label: HBM qualification at Nvidia
kpis.watch: Qualification would break the SK Hynix/Micron duopoly and shift HBM pricing.

kpis.label: Foundry wins at advanced nodes
kpis.watch: A credible second source at N2+ is the only TSMC hedge.

companies.readThrough: Samsung is the chain's structural swing supplier: its HBM and foundry progress decides whether 2027 bottlenecks loosen.

companies.name: ASE Technology Holding
companies.role: The world's largest outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider. Advanced packaging is no longer only TSMC's CoWoS — the OSAT ecosystem handles test, bumping and fan-out that every AI chip needs.

kpis.label: Advanced packaging revenue
kpis.watch: Tracks AI chip unit volumes in the supply chain that isn't TSMC.

kpis.label: Utilisation
kpis.watch: High utilisation with tight supply = pricing power.

companies.readThrough: ASE is the packaging layer's second source — its capacity additions measure how fast the industry can open non-TSMC packaging lanes.

companies.name: Amkor Technology
companies.role: The largest US-headquartered OSAT, building advanced packaging capacity in Arizona as a direct hedge against Taiwanese/Taiwanese-strait concentration.

kpis.label: US capacity buildout
kpis.watch: Arizona capacity is the physical de-risking signal, not a headline.

kpis.label: Advanced packaging mix
kpis.watch: AI packaging carries premium margins vs. consumer.

companies.readThrough: Amkor is the geopolitical hedge inside the packaging node — watch it as a policy-driven beneficiary.

companies.name: Arista Networks
companies.role: The leading Ethernet switch vendor for hyperscale AI clusters (Meta, Microsoft). Its systems sit on Broadcom silicon — Arista sells the network, Broadcom sells the switching logic inside it.

kpis.label: AI networking revenue
kpis.watch: The clearest revenue line showing Ethernet gaining AI share from InfiniBand.

kpis.label: Hyperscaler concentration
kpis.watch: Two customers dominate; watch programme shifts.

companies.readThrough: Arista reads the network's role in AI: when clusters scale out, Ethernet switch demand follows, quarter by quarter.

companies.name: Celestica
companies.role: Hyperscaler ODM building switches and servers — the North American, non-Taiwanese assembly alternative (with plants in Mexico) at the centre of the geographic de-risking trade.

kpis.label: AI programme revenue
kpis.watch: AI hardware mix is the whole story; margin discipline is the risk.

kpis.label: Non-China capacity
kpis.watch: Mexico capacity is the geopolitical hedge in action.

companies.readThrough: Celestica is the assembler alternative to Taiwan — watch it as the quantified 'Friend-shoring' beneficiary.

companies.name: Coherent
companies.role: Optical transceivers, lasers and photonics for 800G/1.6T data-centre links — the physical light path between GPUs, alongside Marvell's DSPs.

kpis.label: Datacom revenue growth
kpis.watch: Tracks cluster scale-out directly.

kpis.label: 1.6T ramp
kpis.watch: Each speed generation resets supplier share.

companies.readThrough: Optics is the unsung bottleneck: compute slows when transceivers run short.

companies.name: Lumentum
companies.role: EML lasers and optical components underpinning the transceivers inside AI clusters; a key source of the lasers that competitors of Coherent also buy.

kpis.label: Datacom growth
kpis.watch: Cloud bookings are the demand read.

kpis.label: Laser supply tightness
kpis.watch: Scarce lasers = pricing power; easing = margin compression.

companies.readThrough: Lumentum is an upstream leak in the optics layer — its laser supply constrains every transceiver maker.

companies.name: Fabrinet
companies.role: Contract manufacturer of optical modules — builds transceivers for the module vendors and increasingly for AI programmes directly. The 'TSMC of optics assembly'.

kpis.label: Datacom revenue mix
kpis.watch: When optical volumes rise, Fabrinet ships first.

kpis.label: Customer concentration
kpis.watch: One programme can dominate the P&L.

companies.readThrough: Fabrinet's throughput is the cleanest physical read on optical module demand.

companies.name: GE Vernova
companies.role: Gas turbines for on-site data-centre generation plus a grid-equipment franchise (transformers, switchgear, HVDC) inside Electrification. Possibly the single largest listed beneficiary of the AI power crunch, after Eaton/Schneider.

kpis.label: Electrification orders/backlog
kpis.watch: Order growth past 2028 visibility is the transformer bottleneck in numbers.

kpis.label: Gas turbine slot reservations
kpis.watch: Reserved slots = data-centre demand made concrete.

companies.readThrough: GE Vernova sits exactly where the chain's two scarcest physical goods meet: power generation and grid equipment.

companies.name: Hitachi
companies.role: Owner of Hitachi Energy, the global leader in high-voltage transformers and HVDC — one of the three companies that decide how fast the grid can physically connect data centres.

kpis.label: Energy segment orders
kpis.watch: HVDC order wins are multi-year revenue locks.

kpis.label: Transformer lead times
kpis.watch: Extended lead times equal pricing power across the node.

companies.readThrough: Hitachi Energy is the transformer chokepoint in listed form — watch it for the real grid-capacity timeline.

companies.name: Siemens Energy
companies.role: Grid Technologies (transformers, switchgear, HVDC) plus gas services and a troubled wind unit. The European-listed grid-capacity play next to Hitachi and GE Vernova.

kpis.label: Grid Technologies orders
kpis.watch: Orders convert to revenue 2-4 years out; the backlog is the asset.

kpis.label: Wind turnaround
kpis.watch: Wind losses are the discount mechanism for the grid business.

companies.readThrough: Siemens Energy is a cleaner grid proxy if you can stomach the wind-drag — watch the segment mix.

companies.name: Quanta Services
companies.role: North America's largest grid-construction contractor: builds the transmission lines and substations that connect new load. The labour-and-execution bottleneck behind every grid announcement.

kpis.label: Total backlog
kpis.watch: Record backlogs show the buildout is physical work, not just approvals.

kpis.label: Data-centre related work
kpis.watch: Direct disclosure of AI demand would re-rate the story.

companies.readThrough: Quanta monetises the grid buildout with less commodity and valuation risk than the equipment makers.

companies.name: Caterpillar
companies.role: Diesel and gas generator sets for data-centre backup and on-site power — every rack hall ships with CAT gensets as the last line of defence.

kpis.label: Energy & transportation sales
kpis.watch: Genset demand from data centres is the new growth line.

kpis.label: Dealer inventory / cycle
kpis.watch: The construction cycle remains the anchor risk.

companies.readThrough: Caterpillar is a lower-beta, dividend-paying way to own the 'every megawatt needs a backup' trade.

companies.name: Talen Energy
companies.role: Nuclear IPP whose Susquehanna campus powers Amazon's data-centre complex directly — the second name, after Constellation, proving the co-location nuclear model.

kpis.label: Co-location/PPA announcements
kpis.watch: Each deal locks premium fixed revenue.

kpis.label: PJM capacity market rules
kpis.watch: Changes to co-location rules can move the whole model.

companies.readThrough: Talen validates the nuclear co-location template beyond Constellation — the cheapest baseload in the chain.

companies.name: nVent Electric
companies.role: Liquid-cooling cold plates, manifolds and electrical enclosures — the component-level thermal supplier behind liquid conversions, alongside Vertiv, Modine and Schneider.

kpis.label: Data solutions growth
kpis.watch: Liquid cooling adjacency is the growth engine.

kpis.label: Electrical connections backlog
kpis.watch: Product-level demand tracks rack builds.

companies.readThrough: nVent supplies the hardware inside the cooling loop — the fourth cooling name completes the picture.

companies.name: Nebius Group
companies.role: European neocloud (ex-Yandex assets) renting GPU capacity to AI labs; one of the group that collapsed ~30% in the October 2026 sell-off. The EU-listed alternative in the leverage layer.

kpis.label: Contracted ARR
kpis.watch: Backlog conversion is the whole investment case.

kpis.label: Financing terms
kpis.watch: Cost of capital decides the business model.

companies.readThrough: Nebius makes the neocloud group a peer set — watch its financing terms against CoreWeave's for the credit cycle read.

companies.name: IREN
companies.role: Bitcoin miner converting power sites into AI cloud capacity — the clearest example of the 'power is the asset, GPUs are the product' pivot.

kpis.label: AI cloud revenue
kpis.watch: The pivot's success measure against mining revenue.

kpis.label: Power capacity secured
kpis.watch: Megawatts under contract are the moat.

companies.readThrough: IREN tracks the miner-to-AI conversion trade — a high-beta proxy for data-centre power scarcity.

companies.name: Intel
companies.role: The only US company that both designs processors and attempts leading-edge fabrication. Xeon still powers much of the cloud, but the accelerator race and the foundry buildout went badly — which makes Intel the chain's cheapest call option on non-Taiwan leading-edge capacity. Q3 2026 beat (revenue $16.5B, +21% YoY; data centre/AI +78%), yet the stock collapsed ~25.6% (~$125B of value) on Oct 30 after weak Q4 PC guidance — memory-price inflation is forcing PC makers to slash inventories — compounded by a fatal fab incident in Israel.
upstream: memory suppliers (ironically: DRAM inflation hurts its PC customers)

kpis.label: Foundry external customers
kpis.watch: One credible external customer would re-rate the foundry thesis; none material yet.

kpis.label: Free cash flow
kpis.value: Guidance still does not forecast positive FCF
kpis.watch: Intel needs cash for the buildout; negative FCF plus capex is the existential risk.

kpis.label: PC cycle vs memory inflation
kpis.value: Q4 guide cut on memory-driven inventory cuts
kpis.watch: DRAM/HBM demand is starving PC margins — watch whether that eases in 2027.

companies.readThrough: Intel is the chain's value/turnaround expression: if US leading-edge capacity becomes strategic enough to fund, the option pays enormously; if not, it keeps burning cash while TSMC takes the margin. Watch foundry wins, not headlines.
risks: Long execution history of missed roadmaps
Policy dependence (~10% US government stake since 2025)

sources.title: Intel Q3 2026 beat, Q4 guide shock, -25.6% Oct 30

lastReport.headline: Q3 beat (revenue $16.5B, +21%) but weak Q4 guide ($15-16B vs ~$17.1B)
lastReport.reaction: −25.6% (~$125B of value), worst day since 1974 territory
lastReport.summary: Memory-price inflation is forcing PC inventory cuts; a fatal Israel fab incident costs $300-600M; guidance does not forecast positive FCF. The foundry thesis now rests on external customers that don't yet exist.

companies.name: SanDisk
companies.role: Pure-play NAND flash, spun out of Western Digital in 2025 and repositioned as the AI-storage supplier: enterprise SSDs and high-density QLC flash for inference caches. Its new multi-year 'NVM' supply contracts with hyperscalers (reported total value $42-94B, durations up to five years, financial guarantees) are an attempt to tame NAND's legendary cycle. NAND joint venture with Kioxia extended through 2034.
upstream: Kioxia (JV fabs in Yokkaichi and Kitakami)
customers: US hyperscalers (3 in the NVM programme reportedly)

kpis.label: NVM contract coverage
kpis.value: Contracts reportedly cover ~1/3 of FY2027 bit shipments
kpis.watch: If multi-year contracts hold through the next downturn, NAND's cycle has genuinely changed; if they get renegotiated, it has not.

kpis.label: NAND pricing
kpis.value: ASPs up ~140% QoQ in 2026; enterprise SSD shortage
kpis.watch: Pricing power this extreme invites capacity — watch for the first supply response.

kpis.label: Data-centre share of NAND demand
kpis.watch: The structural demand shift behind the shortage; inference caches are the new storage workload.

companies.readThrough: Storage stopped being the boring commodity of the chain: AI inference reads exabytes, and NAND now has backlog visibility for the first time. SanDisk is the cleanest listed expression of that transition — and its contract structure is the experiment to watch.
risks: NAND cycle is not dead, only contracted
Premium valuation (~6x forward sales at the peak)

companies.name: Kioxia Holdings
companies.role: Japan's NAND champion and the third global NAND producer, tied to SanDisk through the Yokkaichi/Kitakami joint ventures. Supplies the flash inside enterprise SSDs — the storage tier under every inference workload.

kpis.label: JV output and roadmap
kpis.watch: Bits-per-wafer growth on 13% of industry capex was the JV's historic edge — watch it hold.

kpis.label: NAND pricing
kpis.watch: Kioxia's earnings are the cleanest read on NAND spot economics in Asia.

companies.readThrough: Kioxia is SanDisk's twin: same fabs, same shortage, different listing. Owning both is owning one business twice — pick one if you size it.

companies.name: Seagate Technology
companies.role: The nearline HDD leader for data centres — storage is the third pillar of AI infrastructure after compute and power. Nearline capacity is fully allocated through calendar 2026, long-term agreements with cloud customers run through 2027, and customers are already discussing 2028-29 demand. Roughly 90% of Seagate's exabyte shipments go to data centres; growth comes from areal density (HAMR), not more units.
customers: hyperscalers (AWS, Google, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI-class buyers)

kpis.label: Nearline allocation
kpis.value: Fully allocated through 2026; H1 2027 orders being taken
kpis.watch: The shortage is the moat: watch the first year a hyperscaler gets unallocated supply.

kpis.label: Areal density roadmap
kpis.watch: Capacity per drive is the growth lever in a no-new-units model.

kpis.label: Exabyte growth
kpis.watch: Exabyte CAGR is the honest AI-demand read for storage.

companies.readThrough: HDDs were the most boring asset in tech until AI recycled them. The shortage now shows up as 52+ week lead times — storage tightness is as physical as transformers and chillers.
risks: SSD substitution at the high end

sources.title: WD & Seagate confirm 2026 drives sold out (heise)

companies.name: Western Digital
companies.role: HDD-only since the SanDisk spin-off: nearline drive maker, sold out through calendar 2026, long-term agreements with most top customers into 2027-28 (customers already negotiating 2030-31 assurance). Roadmap runs from 44TB drives now toward 100TB by 2029, targeting >25% exabyte CAGR.

kpis.label: LTA coverage
kpis.value: Most 2027 supply under long-term agreements; 2028/29 signed
kpis.watch: Contract length is the visibility metric — and the pricing-power proof.

kpis.label: Gross margin
kpis.value: 46.1% in the FY2025 Q4 print (up from 38.4%)
kpis.watch: Margin expansion on fixed capacity is the whole earnings story.

kpis.label: Density roadmap
kpis.watch: Dell's COO expects component tightness 5+ years, memory and HDD the worst — watch his supply commentary.

companies.readThrough: Western Digital and Seagate are effectively a duopoly-plus-Toshiba on nearline capacity; both sold out into 2027 is the storage equivalent of transformers being sold out to 2028.
risks: SSD price crossover could cap upside

sources.title: Hard drives sold out for the year (The Register)

companies.name: Oracle
companies.role: The debt-financed hyperscaler: OCI won enormous AI compute contracts (OpenAI/Stargate-class programmes) and is building capacity at a pace its cash flow doesn't cover. Oracle carries both the chain's biggest visible AI backlog and its most acute financing risk — 5-year CDS at an 18-year high, S&P rating at BBB-.

kpis.label: RPO (remaining performance obligations)
kpis.watch: The backlog is the bull case; watch conversion pace and contract quality.

kpis.label: Capex vs. free cash flow
kpis.watch: Oracle is the first hyperscaler where negative FCF is structural, not cyclical.

kpis.label: CDS spread / bond spreads
kpis.watch: The single best real-time gauge of AI-credit stress — if Oracle breaks, the funding-shock scenario starts.

companies.readThrough: Oracle is the chain's leveraged bet on AI demand: a database business funding a compute buildout for customers who may or may not pay up. Its credit metrics are the canary for the whole debt layer.

sources.title: Oracle credit stress reporting (CDS 18-yr high, BBB-)

companies.name: Dell Technologies
companies.role: One of the largest AI server and storage system vendors (PowerEdge/ISG) for hyperscalers and enterprises — the scale OEM next to SMCI and the Taiwanese ODMs. Thin margins, huge revenue: the 'value' way to own AI hardware volumes rather than pricing power.

kpis.label: AI server orders/backlog
kpis.watch: Dell's AI backlog is a demand cross-check on SMCI and the ODMs.

kpis.label: ISG margin
kpis.watch: AI server mix is margin-dilutive — the ODM trap applies to Dell too.

companies.readThrough: Dell's AI backlog and margin tell you whether the physical buildout is broadening from hyperscalers to enterprises — the demand question that matters for 2027.

companies.name: Astera Labs
companies.role: Connectivity silicon for AI racks: PCIe/CXL retimers and the Scorpio fabric switches that connect GPUs to each other and to CPU/memory inside the rack. Every GPU added raises connectivity content — one of the fastest-growing subnodes of the chain. Market cap ~$50-68B in Oct 2026, then -26% in the selloff: the definition of a high-beta AI name.

kpis.label: Scorpio ramp
kpis.watch: Scale-up fabric wins decide whether Astera becomes a standard or a niche.

kpis.label: Customer concentration
kpis.watch: A few hyperscalers carry revenue; one design change can move the stock 20%.

companies.readThrough: Astera quantifies how connectivity content per rack compounds with GPU count — the clearest public read on scale-up networking demand.

companies.name: Credo Technology
companies.role: Active electrical cables (AECs) and SerDes IP for 400G/800G/1.6T links — the copper answer to optics inside and between racks, cheaper and lower-power for short runs. ~$32-34B market cap on ~$1.3B revenue, de-rated -23% in the October sell-off.

kpis.label: Revenue growth
kpis.watch: AEC adoption tracks cluster build rates; growth slowing is an early crack.

kpis.label: Optics competition
kpis.watch: When co-packaged optics matures, copper's reach shrinks — the structural cap on the thesis.

companies.readThrough: Credo is the copper half of the interconnect trade; Marvell/Coherent are the optical half. Watching both tells you where the bandwidth bottleneck is moving.

companies.name: Digital Realty
companies.role: Data-centre REIT — the landlord layer: owns and leases colocation and interconnection capacity to hyperscalers and enterprises (Equinix is the closest peer). Structural demand from AI; levered, rate-sensitive, and priced off the 10-year, which sits near 5%.

kpis.label: Bookings and backlog
kpis.watch: AI leasing demand is real; watch pricing power at renewals.

kpis.label: Cost of capital
kpis.watch: REITs are duration: rates up 100bp ≈ multiple compression, whatever AI demand does.

companies.readThrough: Digital Realty is the only way in this list to own the land-and-power layer as a REIT — but at 5% long rates, the financing tide runs against it.

interdependencies.title: 1 · The capex loop: hyperscalers feed Nvidia
interdependencies.body: Big Tech capex guidance is the demand signal for the entire hardware layer. Microsoft guides ~$170B for FY2027; Amazon ~$220B for 2026 with 2027 'significantly' higher; Alphabet spends $51.4B per quarter with 2027 guided significantly above its $195-205B 2026 range; Meta raised 2026 capex to $135-145B. A large share of that flows straight into Nvidia: Q2 FY2027 revenue was $96.2B, of which $89.0B (92.6%) was data center — split $48.7B hyperscale (+102% YoY) and $40.3B ACIE (AI clouds, industrial, enterprise; +139%). The ACIE segment growing faster than hyperscale is the structural change to watch: the chain is diversifying beyond Big Tech, into debt-funded buyers.

interdependencies.title: 2 · Equity + compute loops: labs and their landlords
interdependencies.body: Microsoft holds ~27% of the OpenAI Group and rents it Azure compute; Amazon and Google both hold Anthropic stakes and are its primary cloud providers — so a dollar of Anthropic funding partially recycles into AWS/GCP revenue. October 2026 added a new loop: with Meta raising $95B in equity, Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom each expressed interest in buying up to $5B of the shares — chip vendors financing their own customers. Each loop boosts reported growth today and concentrates correlated risk later.

interdependencies.title: 3 · The debt layer: neoclouds as the marginal buyer
interdependencies.body: Neoclouds (CoreWeave and peers) borrow against GPUs to buy more GPUs, and they are a large part of Nvidia's ACIE demand. This is the chain's leverage layer: their backlog confirms AI demand is real, while their bond yields measure how nervous credit markets are. The group fell sharply (~-30% reported) in the October 2026 sell-off. Bank of America's takeaway from the month: 'the era of big buybacks is over' — Big Tech bonds may offer better risk-adjusted exposure than the stocks.

interdependencies.title: 4 · The funding bill comes due: free cash flow goes negative
interdependencies.body: October 2026 was the month capex outran cash generation at three of the four hyperscalers: Alphabet FCF -$9.07B (capex $51.4B, buybacks halted, equity issued), Amazon TTM FCF -$42.4B (Q3 capex $77.3B), Meta FCF -$2.12B — its first shortfall in over a decade — and a $95B equity raise ($35B public offering + up to $60B ATM). Microsoft stayed positive (+$18.6B FCF on $45.2B quarterly capex). The market's reaction: Alphabet -13.7% (largest single-day drop on record), Amazon -7.5%, Intel -25.6% (~$125B of value) on weak PC guidance compounded by memory-price inflation. The correction is not about AI demand failing; it is about the gap between capex and monetization.

interdependencies.title: 5 · The component & assembly chokepoint: Taiwan and the Tier-1/2 suppliers
interdependencies.body: Below the chip layer sits the real physical bottleneck the first overview missed: IC substrates (Ibiden, Unimicron, Tripod), high-density power supplies (Delta, Lite-On), high-speed cabling (Amphenol, Marvell), cooling hardware (Vertiv, Modine, AAON) — and the Taiwanese ODMs (Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron) that assemble over 90% of advanced AI server racks. A modern AI rack draws over 100kW against ~10kW for a traditional cloud rack, so air cooling cannot cope and every rack needs liquid-cooling loops, precision manifolds and leak-proof couplings (Stäubli and Boyd, both private). Lead times for high-voltage transformers and data-centre chillers stretch 2-3 years and backlogs run past 2028, which gives this layer unusual pricing power. The catch is geography: even a US cooling company cannot ship a finished unit if Taiwanese subcontractors cannot deliver the chassis power shelves and micro-valves. Owning Western-domiciled infrastructure (Vertiv US, Schneider France, Eaton Ireland) hedges equity exposure to the Taiwan Strait, but it does not remove the operational dependency.

interdependencies.title: 6 · The storage tier: AI eats exabytes, not just FLOPS
interdependencies.body: The chain's most recent bottleneck is not silicon but storage. Data centres went from ~20% of NAND bit demand in the early 2020s to ~50% in 2026 — inference reads far more data than training. Enterprise SSDs are short, NAND ASPs rose ~140% QoQ at the peak, and SanDisk has locked hyperscalers into multi-year 'NVM' contracts ($42-94B reported) to dampen the cycle. On the other side of the storage divide, nearline HDDs are sold out through 2026: Seagate is fully allocated with LTAs into 2027 and customers asking about 2028-29, Western Digital has most 2027 supply under long-term agreements and customers negotiating 2030-31 assurance, and lead times stretched past 52 weeks. Dell's COO calls component tightness a 5-year problem with memory and HDDs the worst of it. Storage is now as physical — and as scarce — as transformers and chillers.

Scale asymmetry: a private stake's valuation jump is small next to a multi-trillion-dollar parent; core margin compression (energy, GPU depreciation) easily swamps it.
Cannibalization of core revenue: AI Mode queries monetize worse than classic search; Search revenue grew 12% vs 17% previously — the application layer can eat the cash cow that funds it.

forecast: The great capital rotation: money keeps sloshing around rather than leaving the market — out of premium-priced AI tech into energy, utilities (needed to power data centers) and defensive value.

The Nvidia pressure cooker: hyperscalers say near-term hardware orders are intact, so Nvidia's next quarter likely stays robust. The risk is guidance: any deceleration in demand as budgets get reined in triggers a deeper hardware-layer correction.
The neocloud debt squeeze: specialist AI clouds face intense scrutiny on bond yields and debt levels after their ~30% October drawdown.

The bottom line: the next months bring high volatility and muted valuations for tech. AI stocks are unlikely to reclaim record highs until companies prove they can monetize AI at a margin that covers the data-center bill.

The Taiwan chokepoint remains the tail risk: over 90% of advanced AI rack assembly and much of the micro-component supply sit in the Taiwan Strait. New US and European fabs fix chip supply, not final rack assembly — watch ODM capacity in Mexico/Vietnam/US as the real de-risking signal.

counterpoints.title: 1 · Pricing power is not evenly distributed across the component tier
counterpoints.body: Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron and Super Micro have backlogs but single-digit ODM margins — they are assemblers, not toll collectors. PCBs are competitive. Real scarcity rents sit at substrates, high-end PSUs, chillers and transformers. '2028 backlogs' are also often framework agreements that can slip, and the market has already priced the safety in — Vertiv trades near 50x earnings. The truly insulated cash flows are the utility PPAs, not the component makers.

counterpoints.title: 2 · The geographic hedge is partly domicile theater
counterpoints.body: Holding Vertiv (US), Schneider (France) and Eaton (Ireland) changes currency and listing exposure, not the operating dependency — their components still pass through Taiwanese ODMs and East Asian supply. Only ODM capacity physically moving to Mexico, Vietnam or the US de-risks the chain. Watch Celestica's Mexico lines, Amkor's Arizona packaging and Foxconn's US expansion as the real signals, not the domicile mix.

counterpoints.title: 3 · The demand-side case the dialogue omits
counterpoints.body: Token prices are falling, open-weight models commoditize the 'pixels' layer, and the models layer may earn thin returns while the physical layer captures the economics. That supports the barbell — but for a different reason than 'the hardware always wins': you may be holding the physical layer because the software layer disappoints, not because the buildout is guaranteed. Two different theses, same allocation — know which one you are buying.

counterpoints.title: 4 · EUR/USD is half the five-year question
counterpoints.body: Roughly 70% of the Sparplan's value sits in USD-priced assets held by a German investor. Over five years the exchange rate can contribute or destroy as much as stock selection. The plan is unhedged; EUR strength in a risk-off unwind would compound a tech drawdown. Either accept the USD exposure as a deliberate bet (USD assets, dollar earnings) or lean the European names (Schneider, Siemens, Siemens Energy) in the same sleeves to balance it — but decide consciously. This is the one analysis the Gemini dialogue offered and never delivered.

outlook.stance: Late-cycle expansion inside a rolling correction. The index sits ~2% below its high; the AI complex does not — semis are ~27% off their peak and 96% of semiconductor stocks are more than 20% below their highs. Treat late 2026 / 2027 as a high-volatility regime where contracted cash flow beats beta, and where a ~5% short rate makes cash a legitimate position for the first time in years.
outlook.summary: This is not 2000 on earnings multiples — it is 1999 on concentration, leverage and narrative. S&P earnings grew ~29% in Q3 2026 and the top-5 tech forward P/E (~23x) is a third of the dot-com average (~65x). But the Shiller CAPE (~41 vs 44.2 at the 1999 peak), a 235%+ Buffett indicator, record margin debt ($1.48T) and a credit-financed capex boom ($182B IG issuance YTD; ~$570B AI debt expected) recreate the 2000 playbook on a different axis: the risk is not multiple compression alone, it is a funding event.

council.note: Six investor lenses applied to this model on 2026-10-30 (Buffett, Dalio, Marks, Druckenmiller, Hohn, Serenity). Each verdict, its evidence and its invalidation are written down — that is the difference between using a framework and quoting one. Re-run quarterly and score each lens against outcomes.

verdicts.thesis: The book is one risk factor: AI capex beta. Regime map says growth decelerating + inflation rising (CPI 3.7%, Brent $115) — the stagflation quadrant where concentrated equities and long bonds both struggle, and real assets and cash win on risk contribution.
verdicts.evidence: ~95% of the model's variance is one driver; 15% cash is liquidity, not diversification: zero gold, zero inflation-linked bonds, zero non-AI equity beta. 10y at ~5% gives bonds an actual job for the first time in years.
verdicts.action: Two-layer architecture: diversified core (global equity UCITS + short/intermediate bonds + gold 5-8% + cash) sized 50-60%; AI chain sleeve becomes a satellite of 40-50%. Balance risk contribution, not capital.
verdicts.invalidation: If inflation falls with growth holding (goldilocks), the core can be trimmed; if growth falls with inflation (recession proper), bonds+gold carry the book and the satellite gets bought, not sold.

verdicts.thesis: Real businesses with real moats exist in this sleeve (ASML, TSMC, Microsoft, Eaton, Schneider, regulated utilities). The problem is price: CAPE 41 and semis at ~23-26x forward leave no margin of safety; several names' owner earnings depend on capex financed by debt.
verdicts.evidence: Vertical market leaders with durable advantages, but the AI segment is priced for perfection; the Meta $95B raise and vendor-financed chip purchases are exactly the incentives Buffett distrusts. Cash at 3.5-5% is an acceptable alternative while waiting.
verdicts.action: No new capital into the sleeve at these levels. Keep a written 30%-discount watchlist per name (owner earnings, ROIC > 15%). Only buy fear. Prefer the understandable, cash-generative layer — utilities at fair prices, Eaton, Schneider, ASML — and say 'too hard' to merchant power and leverage stories.
verdicts.invalidation: Earnings compound >25% for 2-3 years so multiples normalise by growth rather than price decline.

verdicts.thesis: Late cycle: easy credit, thin risk premiums, AI mania with pockets of fear. The first-level view is 'AI will be huge'; the second-level view is that the consensus is no longer cheap — what is in the price is perfection. The market is not compensating you for the risk that capex pauses.
verdicts.evidence: Record IG issuance ($182B YTD), Oracle CDS at an 18-year high, covenant-lite-style financing in neoclouds, 96% of semis >20% off highs while the index sits 2% from its record — the classic late-cycle divergence.
verdicts.action: Stay defensive: keep the cash sleeve ≥15%, pre-write the 'buy memo' now (what to buy, at what price, with what thesis), and move from defensive to opportunistic only when spreads widen or forced selling appears. Do not confuse low volatility with low risk.
verdicts.invalidation: Credit spreads stay tight and earnings keep rising — the risk premium gets restored through earnings, not price, and the defensive stance costs carry.

verdicts.thesis: Dominant driver is liquidity tightening + energy shock: 10y ~5%, Fed with a hike bias, oil shock feeding CPI. Price confirms a de-risking regime (semis −27%, breadth weak). There is no liquidity tailwind to press until the Fed changes direction.
verdicts.evidence: Cross-asset confirmation: rates up, dollar firm, small caps weak, credit spreads widening; the AI complex is in a rolling bear market though the index is flat.
verdicts.action: Do not add at size. Hold cash/T-bills, define the expressions for the next regime now: when the Fed pivots or a credit event forces it, press quality AI infrastructure (ASML, TSMC, MSFT) fast. Size down until price confirms.
verdicts.invalidation: Fed pauses without a hike, breadth improves, and semis reclaim their 200-day — then add risk rather than wait for a capitulation that never comes.

verdicts.thesis: Our reverse-mapping matches the professional stacks: the value has rotated from chips to power, components and storage, and the next upstream rotation is photonics / co-packaged optics. But the lens also says: a correct theme with dilution risk still loses money.
verdicts.evidence: Leveraged names (CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN, Oracle) carry ATM/offering overhang; micro-cap bottlenecks (AAOI, SIVE, AXTI-class, AEHR) are where the lens hunts but where our liquidity rule forbids core positions; Meta's $95B raise is dilution in the open.
verdicts.action: Keep the sleeve to verified, liquid bottlenecks (ASML, TSMC, MU/SNDK/STX, VRT, ETN, CEG/GEV/Hitachi). Add a photonics/CPO watch layer in the study — monitor, do not own micro-caps. Check dilution before any new name enters the model.
verdicts.invalidation: CPO adoption slower than the 2027-28 roadmap; or a liquid photonics leader becomes available at a reasonable multiple.

verdicts.thesis: Concentration is earned by quality, not by theme. The Sparplan's eight names are the right order of magnitude, but quality ranks unevenly: monopoly and pricing-power businesses first, commodity-adjacent assemblers last.
verdicts.evidence: ASML (sole EUV), TSMC (foundry scale), Microsoft (switching costs), Eaton/Schneider (pricing power with backlogs) are exceptional; Vertiv is excellent but priced; Modine is the weakest moat of the eight; NVDA's CUDA is real, its cyclicality is too.
verdicts.action: Hold 6-8 names maximum. Quality ordering within sleeves: ASML ≈ TSMC > MSFT > Eaton ≈ Schneider > Vertiv > NVDA (moat yes, cycle yes) > Modine. Consider consolidating Modine into Vertiv or nVent if simplicity matters more than diversification.
verdicts.invalidation: A quality name's ROIC or pricing power breaks structurally (e.g., custom silicon erodes NVDA's share faster than expected).

council.agree: Five of six lenses say the same thing from different doors: be defensive at these prices, treat the AI chain as a satellite and not a core, keep the cash sleeve, and pre-commit what you will buy when the fat pitch comes. Which quality names, at what discount, with what invalidation — written down before the panic.
council.disagree: Dalio wants real diversification (gold, bonds, global equity core) while Serenity and Druckenmiller say concentration is the whole point. The resolution is layering, not choosing: a diversified core sized to survive a −50% satellite, plus the concentrated AI satellite sized so that −50% is survivable. Buffett and Hohn split on price — quality is agreed, margin of safety is not available today.
council.architecture: Two-layer portfolio. CORE (50-60%): global equity UCITS ~35-40%, euro short/intermediate government bonds ~8-10%, gold ETC ~5-8%, cash buffer ~5-8% — the part that survives any scenario. SATELLITE (40-50%): this AI chain model at 35/25/15/10/15, capped so a −50% satellite drawdown costs <25% of total assets. Deployment ladder from the satellite cash: 1/3 at −10% from peak, 1/3 at −20%, 1/3 at −30% or on a confirmed liquidity pivot, each with the pre-written buy list. German execution: UCITS ETFs are the legal wrapper (US ETFs blocked by PRIIPs); the cash sleeve uses €STR or broker cash. Review quarterly, rebalance on ±5pp drift or regime change.

portfolioModel.name: Power & Pixels — stress-aware revision (Oct 2026)
portfolioModel.note: Revised after the October 2026 repricing: a 15% cash/short-treasury sleeve funded by trimming tech, infrastructure and utilities; the barbell alone was never a hedge. The investor council review (Analysis → Council) reframes this model as a SATELLITE of 40-50% of total assets, with a diversified core around it — see the architecture line there.

sleeves.rationale: Still the contractual foundation (fixed-rate PPAs), trimmed from 40% because CEG/VST were repriced as AI proxies: their drawdown beta in a funding shock is real, only their cash flow is not.
Picks and shovels with 2028 backlogs, trimmed from 30% — VRT at ~50x earnings means the safety was priced in; keep the backlog, lose the multiple risk.
Capped at 15% (from 20): semis sit ~27% below their peak; the sleeve is for eventual upside, not current conviction.
Unchanged: the bridge fuel and the one sleeve that benefits if the Hormuz risk premium stays. Cheap multiples, high yields.
New: at ~3.5-5% nominal, cash yields more than the portfolio's dividends and is the only asset that reliably rises when credit breaks. It is also the dry powder that buys the next drawdown.

yieldNotes: The revision lifts the blended yield from ~1.12% to ~1.5% — because cash became the portfolio's highest-yielding sleeve (3.5% vs 1.5% utilities). That is the honest signal about this market: safety now pays more than growth dividends.
The utility multiplier remains: CEG/VST yield only ~0.6-0.7% on price; the payoff is dividend growth from cloud contracts, not current income.
Tech's cash stash is intentional — reinvested into custom silicon and energy leases rather than paid out.
Honesty note: blended sector approximations, not current per-share yields — re-check each name before sizing.
protection: Capped tech sleeve: a further -15% on the $1,500 tech allocation costs $225 — 2.25% of the whole book, not 15%.
Anchored base: $6,000 in power, cooling and gas with multi-year backlogs and physical necessity behind the revenue.
Cash as the real hedge: 15% in short treasuries/money market at ~3.5-5% is the only sleeve with genuinely low correlation to the AI complex — and more yield than the other four combined.
Limits of the model: the infrastructure anchor can fall in a genuine AI-capex unwind; this is a barbell plus cash, not insurance. Size it accordingly.
rebalancing: Quarterly review, plus anytime a sleeve drifts more than 5 percentage points from target.
Cash floor: refill the cash sleeve to 15% when it drops below 10% (i.e. after deploying dry powder in a drawdown); deploy it when it exceeds 20%.
Trim discipline: when tech surges past 20% of the portfolio, cut the excess into utilities, gas or cash — harvest the beta, keep the compounding.
Buying window: during sharp tech corrections, deploy cash and defensive dividends into the high-conviction tech names at deep discounts.
EU access note: US-listed stocks are purchasable by EU retail; US ETFs are not (PRIIPs). Cash side uses €STR money-market UCITS or the broker's own cash rate.

assumptions: Illustration only: constant annualized total returns — utilities 10%, infrastructure 12%, tech 15%, gas 8%, cash 3.5% — compounded with dividends reinvested.
No taxes, no volatility path, no rebalancing: a real €10k will show drawdowns this table never does.

insights.title: Total capital appreciation
insights.body: Without adding a dollar, the structure grows 63.1% over five years to an estimated $16,311 — about 10.3% annualized, dragged down deliberately by the 15% cash sleeve.

insights.body: Annual dividend income grows from $151.50 to $247.10 (+63%) — and it starts from a higher base than before, because cash now pays.

insights.title: The automatic rebalancing effect
insights.body: Dividends from stable sleeves get reinvested into whichever sleeve the brokerage buys — during tech selloffs that means cheaper fractional shares of the growth engines.

insights.title: What the cash sleeve changes
insights.body: The 15% cash sleeve is the dry powder and the only sleeve that rises when credit breaks. In a funding shock the other four fall together — this is the sleeve that lets you buy them.

insights.title: What the table cannot show
insights.body: Constant returns hide the risk that matters: the tech sleeve has historically produced its 15% in bursts around -20% to -35% drawdowns. The 5-year smooth line is a teaching device; the actual path decides who stays invested.

setupSteps.title: 1 · Open the search
setupSteps.body: German brokers index by WKN (Wertpapierkennnummer) or ISIN, not by US tickers. Open Trade Republic or Scalable Capital and tap the search icon.

setupSteps.title: 2 · Search by WKN
setupSteps.body: Type the WKN code from the directory below — not the company name — so the app resolves exactly the intended security.

setupSteps.title: 3 · Create the plan
setupSteps.body: Tap the asset, then 'Create Sparplan' / 'Sparplan einrichten'.

setupSteps.title: 4 · Pick frequency and date
setupSteps.body: Choose Monthly / Monatlich and an execution date right after payday (e.g. the 2nd or 16th of the month).

setupSteps.title: 5 · Enter the amount
setupSteps.body: Enter the euro amount from the directory and confirm. Repeat for the second name in each sleeve.

manualDrip.title: Manual DRIP: the dividend sweep
manualDrip.intro: US brokers can automatically reinvest a dividend into the same stock; German brokers legally cannot do this on an individual-stock Sparplan. The workaround is a manual sweep done twice a year — taxes are already handled at source, so the cash that lands in your account is net.

steps.title: 1 · Let cash accumulate
steps.body: Eaton, Broadcom and Schneider pay quarterly dividends. The 15% US treaty withholding and German Abgeltungsteuer are handled instantly, so the cash landing in your broker account is 100% net.

steps.title: 2 · Sweep twice a year
steps.body: Do not log in for every €1.50 payout — the operational drag is too high. Check your uninvested cash balance every six months.

steps.title: 3 · Raise one Sparplan temporarily
steps.body: If €50 of dividends accumulated, open your top-performing infrastructure plan (e.g. Vertiv or Eaton) and raise that month's budget by €50.

steps.title: 4 · Reset to baseline
steps.body: Once the raised plan executes and consumes the accumulated cash, lower the budget back to its baseline. The profits loop back into compounding at zero transaction fees.

taxShield.title: Before the first dividend: Trade Republic
taxShield.body: Profile → Tax / Steuern → Tax Exemptions / Freistellungsauftrag → enter the amount (up to €1,000 for individuals).

taxShield.title: Before the first dividend: Scalable Capital
taxShield.body: Profile → Products / Produkte → Tax Data / Steuerdaten → set the Freistellungsauftrag.

taxShield.title: What it buys you
taxShield.body: Your broker withholds no German tax on dividends or gains until the €1,000 annual threshold is crossed. If this is your only investment account, set the full €1,000.

econ.title: US midterm elections
econ.expected: Policy outcomes get repriced by sector; historically low index volatility, high single-name dispersion.
econ.chainImpact: AI-regulation risk under a sweep; energy and utilities policy direction; semiconductor China-policy signals.

econ.title: October nonfarm payrolls (08:30 ET)
econ.expected: Consensus mid-range. The market now trades strength as hawkish — a December hike is ~75-85% priced.
econ.chainImpact: Strong print → yields up → CAPE-41 compression; tech beta and neoclouds sell first. Weak print → relief rally, but raises questions about the capex cycle's demand base.

econ.title: October CPI (08:30 ET)
econ.expected: Headline elevated by the oil shock (Brent ~$115; ~3.7% annualized in September); core is the number that matters.
econ.chainImpact: Hot core locks the December hike — every 25bp of expected tightening is another discount-rate strike at AI multiples. Cool print = the relief valve.

econ.title: November nonfarm payrolls (08:30 ET)
econ.expected: Second jobs print before the December FOMC; wage growth is the hawkish tell.
econ.chainImpact: Same channel as November's print, amplified by proximity to the Fed decision.

econ.title: FOMC meeting begins
econ.expected: Two-day meeting; no statement on day one.
econ.chainImpact: Positioning day — expect vols to rise into the decision.

econ.title: FOMC decision + dot plot (14:00 ET)
econ.expected: Hike ~75-85% priced. The Summary of Economic Projections (dots) decides the 2027 path.
econ.chainImpact: The single biggest scheduled risk for the stress-aware model (15% cash / 35% utilities): hike + hawkish dots forces the rotation into cash and power; a dovish surprise fuels the melt-up scenario.

econ.title: November CPI (08:30 ET)
econ.expected: Follow-through print the day after the Fed decision.
econ.chainImpact: Post-decision confirmation — a hot print re-prices 2027 hikes and hits duration-sensitive AI names.

econ.title: November PPI (08:30 ET)
econ.chainImpact: Secondary — matters only if it diverges from CPI.

econ.title: November PCE (08:30 ET)
econ.expected: The Fed's preferred gauge; holiday-week liquidity makes reactions exaggerated.
econ.chainImpact: Low-liquidity print — outsized moves possible in the last week of the year.
